Hey everyone! I have a quick question regarding EU registration at Finnish Immigration Service. Is it true that I can book an appointment in any of their offices to register my right of residence? 

The reason I am asking is that I live in Espoo, and the soonest time to attend the office in Helsinki is in the mid-November. That’s why I started considering attending the office in Lahti, where the soonest possible appointment is in the beginning of September. However, when booking an appointment on Migri.fi, I noticed the following note (attached screenshot). 

Is this note is made just to specify that the only office in Helsinki is IHH or that I cannot register my right of residence in other offices?

Finnish Immigration Service - Bytes Europe

# Finnish Immigration Service

August 22, 2024

 

Hey everyone! I have a quick question regarding EU registration at Finnish Immigration Service. Is it true that I can book an appointment in any of their offices to register my right of residence? 

The reason I am asking is that I live in Espoo, and the soonest time to attend the office in Helsinki is in the mid-November. That’s why I started considering attending the office in Lahti, where the soonest possible appointment is in the beginning of September. However, when booking an appointment on Migri.fi, I noticed the following note (attached screenshot). 

Is this note is made just to specify that the only office in Helsinki is IHH or that I cannot register my right of residence in other offices?

Thanks in advance!

sources.title: International House Helsinki Relocates to Pasila ‘Suomi-piste’ Service Hub
highlights: Helsinki’s one-stop service centre for newcomers, International House Helsinki (IHH), opened its doors this morning at a new address—Ratapihantie 7 in the rapidly developing Pasila business district. The relocation, effective 1 June 2026, brings IHH under the roof of the government’s brand-new Suomi-piste (“Finland-Point”) customer-service concept, which gathers multiple public bodies in a single accessible building next to Pasila rail station. IHH is best known among expatriates and global mobility teams for handling EU-citizen registration appointments, issuing Finnish personal identity codes, and providing multilingual advice on taxation, social security and local employment rules. All these services continue unchanged, but visitors now benefit from extended opening hours (09:00–16:00 Monday-Wednesday and Friday; 10:30–16:00 Thursday), barrier-free access and direct rail links to Helsinki Airport and city-centre hotels. According to the Finnish Immigration Service, the move is part of a broader digital-first overhaul of customer service. The Suomi-piste model co-locates Migri desk officers with staff from the Tax Administration, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) and the Social Insurance Institution (Kela). New arrivals can therefore register their right of residence, obtain a tax card, apply for a social-security number and receive orientation counselling in a single visit. For employers, the consolidation promises faster onboarding of foreign hires. Whereas previously an assignee might have needed three separate appointments across town, HR teams can now book one time slot through Migri’s online system and track progress via Enter Finland. Early feedback from pilot users indicates that average time-to-ID-number issuance has dropped from ten days to three. Companies should update welcome packs, relocation guides and map links immediately. The old IHH premises on Lintulahdenkuja will close permanently and no longer accept walk-in visitors. Those with appointments booked before 1 June have been automatically re-scheduled to the Pasila site, and confirmation messages have been sent to the email address on file.

International House Helsinki Relocates to Pasila ‘Suomi-piste’ Service Hub

# International House Helsinki Relocates to Pasila ‘Suomi-piste’ Service Hub

 Jun 2, 2026

 Finn Visas & Immigration Team @ VisaHQ

 Helsinki’s one-stop service centre for newcomers, International House Helsinki (IHH), opened its doors this morning at a new address—Ratapihantie 7 in the rapidly developing Pasila business district. The relocation, effective 1 June 2026, brings IHH under the roof of the government’s brand-new Suomi-piste (“Finland-Point”) customer-service concept, which gathers multiple public bodies in a single accessible building next to Pasila rail station. IHH is best known among expatriates and global mobility teams for handling EU-citizen registration appointments, issuing Finnish personal identity codes, and providing multilingual advice on taxation, social security and local employment rules. All these services continue unchanged, but visitors now benefit from extended opening hours (09:00–16:00 Monday-Wednesday and Friday; 10:30–16:00 Thursday), barrier-free access and direct rail links to Helsinki Airport and city-centre hotels. According to the Finnish Immigration Service, the move is part of a broader digital-first overhaul of customer service. The Suomi-piste model co-locates Migri desk officers with staff from the Tax Administration, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency (DVV) and the Social Insurance Institution (Kela). New arrivals can therefore register their right of residence, obtain a tax card, apply for a social-security number and receive orientation counselling in a single visit. For employers, the consolidation promises faster onboarding of foreign hires. Whereas previously an assignee might have needed three separate appointments across town, HR teams can now book one time slot through Migri’s online system and track progress via Enter Finland. Early feedback from pilot users indicates that average time-to-ID-number issuance has dropped from ten days to three. Companies should update welcome packs, relocation guides and map links immediately. The old IHH premises on Lintulahdenkuja will close permanently and no longer accept walk-in visitors. Those with appointments booked before 1 June have been automatically re-scheduled to the Pasila site, and confirmation messages have been sent to the email address on file. 

 Source: Finnish Immigration Service – Service Point Directory

sources.text:
Moving to Helsinki (2026): The Complete Relocation Guide - Flyto

## Moving to Helsinki (2026): The Complete Relocation Guide

Author: Flyto Editorial Team · Reviewed by: Ariel Keisa, Founder & CEO in

Last reviewed: 7.9.2026

Helsinki is Finland’s capital and by far its largest city — around 675,000 people in the city itself and roughly 1.6 million across the greater Helsinki region — and it is the country’s main landing point for international arrivals. It is also a genuinely Nordic city to move into: much of the desirable housing sits in early-1900s Jugend blocks and 1950s walk-ups with no lift and tight stairwells, the classic city block wraps around an inner courtyard, your moving truck cannot simply reserve the kerb outside the door, and for a large part of the year the loading itself happens on snow and ice in the dark. This guide covers the practical mechanics of moving to Helsinki in 2026 — the truck-and-building logistics only a mover knows, where to live and what rent really costs, how to find a flat and register at DVV, and what monthly life actually costs — with official sources throughout.

Freshness note: prices and rules verified against hel.fi, suomi.fi, dvv.fi, International House Helsinki, HSL, Tilastokeskus, the Finnish Meteorological Institute and Helsinki city statistics in 2026. Fees and rents move — confirm figures with the linked authorities before you rely on them.

## Quick answer: moving to Helsinki in 2026

What does it cost to move to Helsinki? An international household move (a full flat) typically lands in the low-to-mid four figures from within Europe and higher from overseas, driven mostly by volume, distance and access. Because Helsinki’s access difficulties — no-lift Jugend buildings, courtyards, winter conditions — add real cost, get a fixed quote for your specific address rather than a generic estimate: get a Flyto quote here.

How long does the move take? Road moves from within the EU are usually a few days to about two weeks door-to-door; overseas sea freight runs several weeks. The two Helsinki-specific quirks everyone underestimates: nearly half of the city’s apartment buildings have no lift (Helsinki city statistics), so a bulky sofa often has to go in through a window on an external furniture lift (muuttonostin); and there is no free ”book a spot” for the truck — for a disruptive move you take out a paid permit to use the public area (City of Helsinki area-use permit).

## Key takeaways

- Nearly half of Helsinki’s apartment buildings have no lift. At the end of 2018 about 46% of the city’s apartment buildings — roughly 4,900 buildings holding some 90,000 flats — had no elevator, most of them older or mid-century walk-ups (Helsinki city statistics). This is exactly why an external furniture lift (muuttonostin / ulkohissi) is so often needed.
- Your moving truck cannot just reserve the kerb. You may briefly stop to load bulky items, but for a genuinely disruptive move you need a paid permit to take a street or public area into temporary use, granted by the Urban Environment Division (suomi.fi; application via hel.fi).
- Winter is a real operational factor. Permanent snow cover in the capital region normally sets in only after Christmas and clears on average around the turn of March–April (Finnish Meteorological Institute) — snow, ice and short, dark days make winter loading slower and worth planning carefully.
- Register at DVV to get your kotikunta and henkilötunnus. Newcomers register in the Population Information System at DVV — in Helsinki mainly by appointment at International House Helsinki — where you also apply for a personal identity code (henkilötunnus) and municipality of residence (kotikunta), which unlocks public healthcare, daycare and much else (International House Helsinki).
- Deposit is capped and usually 1–2 months. A rental deposit (vuokravakuus) is legally limited to at most three months’ rent (Act on Residential Leases, §8), and in practice landlords typically ask for one to two months (Vuokralaiset ry).

## 1. The move into Helsinki — logistics only a mover knows

This is the part generic ”moving to Helsinki” guides skip, and it is exactly where a move goes wrong. Helsinki’s inner districts were built for courtyards and trams, not for a full-size removal truck, and half the year the weather is against you. Four things determine whether your move day runs smoothly.

### Parking the truck: the loading exception and the area-use permit

Helsinki does not offer a simple online ”book a moving-van bay” service, and you cannot count on a free stretch of kerb outside the building. There are two legal routes:

- The brief loading exception. A vehicle may stop even on a footway or cycle path for the short time it takes to load or unload, but only when there is a compelling reason, the load is genuinely bulky (furniture, white goods, a piano — not hand-carried boxes), at least one metre is left clear for pedestrians, and the driver stays with the vehicle ready to move it (City of Helsinki, ”Sujuvaa pysäköintiä”). This covers a quick, simple move — it does not reserve you a space.
- The area-use permit. For a demanding move that will block a traffic lane or occupy a parking space for longer, you apply for a permit to take a public area into temporary use (lupa yleisen alueen käyttöön) from the Urban Environment Division. The service is paid, the same office that handles street works and events grants it, and you can arrange temporary no-parking signs to keep the space clear (suomi.fi; application form and contact hel.fi, luvat@hel.fi).

Knowing which route your address needs — and arranging the permit and signs in advance when it does — is the difference between a truck parked at the door and one stranded a block away.

### Winter: snow, ice, darkness and frozen loading

This is the genuinely Nordic factor. In the Helsinki region, permanent snow cover typically arrives only after Christmas and disappears on average around the turn of March and April (Finnish Meteorological Institute), but sub-zero spells, ice and slush can bracket that window from November into April. A winter move means snow and ice on the access routes and courtyard, ramps and pavements that need clearing and gritting before anything heavy is carried, daylight that in December runs to only about six hours, and cold that makes long carries and lift set-up slower. None of this stops a move — Finns move house all winter — but it has to be planned for: earlier start times, clearing and salting the path, protecting floors from meltwater and grit, and allowing more time. A mover who works Helsinki winters builds this in; a generic van hire discovers it at 8 a.m. on a frozen loading bay.

### Jugend blocks, 1950s walk-ups and the muuttonostin

Much of the housing people actually want in Helsinki sits in early-1900s Jugend (Art Nouveau) blocks in Kruununhaka, Ullanlinna, Eira, Punavuori and Katajanokka, or in the 1950s rintamamiestalo-era walk-ups further out. Many of these buildings have no lift, and where a lift exists it is often a small original cage that will not take a wardrobe. Citywide, roughly 46% of apartment buildings had no elevator at the end of 2018 — about 4,900 buildings and 90,000 flats (Helsinki city statistics).

The practical consequence: sofas, wardrobes, double beds and appliances frequently will not fit up a narrow, turning Helsinki stairwell. The standard solution is an external furniture lift (muuttonostin / ulkohissi) — a ladder hoist run up the facade to bring bulky items in through a window or balcony, reaching the upper floors and attic conversions. It needs its own space at the kerb, which is another reason the parking arrangement matters. A good mover measures the stairwell, the floor and the doorways before the day and books the lift in advance, rather than discovering the problem when the sofa is wedged on the second-floor landing.

### Courtyards, gate arches and one-way streets

The classic Helsinki block is built around an inner courtyard (sisäpiha), reached through a gate arch (porttikäytävä) that is usually too low and too narrow for a truck to enter. A flat in the courtyard wing (piharakennus) can mean carrying every box a long way from the street, across the yard, and the yard itself is often reserved for residents’ parking and bins. Add the peninsula’s one-way streets, tram tracks and cycle lanes, and ”just park outside” is rarely simple. None of this is a problem if it is planned for — and all of it is a bad surprise if it is not.

## 2. Where to live — Helsinki neighborhoods by profile

Helsinki’s character changes district by district, and the water is never far. The figures below are indicative average asking rents (€/m²/month) for late 2025 from Asunnollehinta.fi, cross-checked against Tilastokeskus rent statistics (Statistics Finland) and Helsinki’s own market review (kaupunkitieto.hel.fi). The citywide average sits around €20/m²; smaller flats cost far more per square metre than large ones, so a studio in a ”cheap” area can still be dear.

Central and characterful:

- Kamppi / Kluuvi — the centre (~€23/m²) — maximum convenience: the main station, metro, trams, shops and offices at the door. You pay the top rents and get little neighbourhood calm; some blocks empty out after work.
- Kruununhaka (~€18/m²) — the dignified old town beside the harbour and university: Jugend and Empire buildings, quiet cobbled streets, older residents and academics. Beautiful and central, mostly no-lift stairwells, and short on nightlife.
- Punavuori (~€21/m²) — the design district: independent shops, cafés and bars in handsome early-1900s blocks. Young professionals and creatives; lively, walkable and pricey, with the usual weekend noise near the bar streets.
- Eira & Ullanlinna (~€17–22/m²) — the seaside establishment: villas, embassies and grand Jugend flats by the shore parks. Prestigious and calm; the per-m² average is pulled down by large family apartments, but small flats are expensive and rare.

Best for young professionals and nightlife:

- Kallio (~€21/m²) — the classic first Helsinki address: small flats, cheap eats and the densest bar scene in the city, historically working-class and now thoroughly mixed. Central and full of life, but noisy and short on space.
- Sörnäinen (~€21/m²) — Kallio’s edgier neighbour by the metro, with the Kalasatama towers and new-build rising nearby; convenient and buzzy, uneven street to street.
- Töölö (~€19–20/m²) — elegant and central, wrapping the bay and the big parks, opera and concert hall: refined 1920s–30s blocks, popular with professionals and families alike. Calmer and greener than Kallio, and priced for it.

Quieter, greener, good value:

- Vallila (~€18/m²) — brick 1920s blocks and a famous wooden-house enclave (Puu-Vallila); down-to-earth, well connected by tram, gentrifying steadily. Good value close to the centre.
- Kumpula & Käpylä (~€17–18/m²) — leafy, low-rise and family-friendly, with garden-city wooden houses and the university campus; calm and green, a little further out, below the city average for larger flats.
- Lauttasaari (~€19/m²) — the popular island suburb one metro stop west: sea on every side, 1950s–60s blocks and newer builds, beaches and quick access to the centre. A favourite of families and remote workers.

Neighbouring cities (same commuter region):

- Espoo — Tapiola (~€19–27/m²) — the western neighbour: green, spacious and family-oriented, home to Aalto University and much of the tech sector. Tapiola is a leafy garden city on the metro; Espoo’s citywide average is close to Helsinki’s (~€20/m²), with Pohjois-Tapiola among the priciest spots (~€27/m²).
- Vantaa (generally below Helsinki, top areas rarely above ~€25/m²) — the northern neighbour around the airport, well linked by the Ring Rail Line; more space for the money, plainer in places, a sensible pick if budget or commute to the airport matters.

sources.title: Moving to Finland – the first 30 days, step by step
highlights:
Several rules changed just before you arrived: since 1 January 2025 you register as a jobseeker with your municipality, not a state TE Office, and on 1 June 2026 International House Helsinki moved to Pasila; part 2 covers the 2025–2026 permit reforms. The order of your first 30 days is unchanged, and it matters.

...

Citizens of the Nordic countries, the EU, Liechtenstein and Switzerland need no residence permit and arrive with a valid identity card or passport. Everyone else applies to Migri (Finnish Immigration Service; Migrationsverket

...

## The first 30 days in Finland, in order

InfoFinland, the official guide run by the City of Helsinki with the ministries, and the agencies themselves give this order; each row has its own part later in the series.

| Step | What | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Settle your right to stay | Migri; DVV for Nordic citizens; a permit before travel for others |
| 2 | Secure an address | Landlord; part 5 |
| 3 | Get the personal identity code, unless Migri issued it | DVV, or a tax office for tax purposes |
| 4 | Apply for a municipality of residence – a separate step | DVV |
| 5 | Get a verokortti (tax card) | Vero (Tax Administration) |
| 6 | Open a bank account; ask for online banking codes | Your bank; part 4 |
| 7 | Tell Kela about your move; apply for the Kela card | OmaKela or form Y 77e |
| 8 | Register as a jobseeker if you have no work | Your municipality’s employment services |
| 9 | Find your terveysasema (health station) | Your hyvinvointialue (wellbeing services county) |
| 10 | Phone, foreigner’s identity card and, if needed, a licence exchange | An operator; the police; Ajovarma |

...

## Week one: your right to stay and where to go

EU citizens staying more than three months register their right of residence with Migri within three months of arrival, only after moving, for 53 euros. Nordic citizens instead register in person at DVV within one month of moving if they stay more than six months. Permit holders get a residence permit card, delivered to a collection point in Finland within about two weeks of the decision; it is not an identity document.

In Helsinki one address covers most of week one. International House Helsinki, at Ratapihantie 7 in Pasila since 1 June 2026, handles EU registration for Migri, the code and municipality of residence for DVV, the tax card for Vero, jobseeker registration and Kela by remote service, Monday to Friday 9.00–16.00. Identity cards are the exception: newcomers go to the Helsinki Police Department at Pasilanraitio 11. Espoo and Vantaa residents use the same house, because DVV’s Espoo office has closed permanently.

| City | Migri service point | DVV service location | Tax office |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Helsinki | Kaupparaitti 10 (Malmi); EU registration also at International House | Ratapihantie 7, floor K1, appointments Mon–Fri 9.00–16.15 | Ratapihantie 7, Mon–Fri 9.00–16.00 |
| Tampere | Tekniikankatu 1, wing A | Hatanpään valtatie 36, appointments Tue–Fri 9.00–16.00 | Hatanpään valtatie 36 |
| Turku | Nallinkatu 8 in Raisio – none in Turku itself | Kulttuurikuja 1, Mon–Fri 9.00–16.00 | Kulttuurikuja 1, Suomi-piste |
| Oulu | Albertinkatu 4 B | Viestikatu 1, Tue–Wed and Fri 9.00–16.00 | Uusikatu 52 |

Source: Migri, DVV and the Finnish Tax Administration, read 24 September 2026.

## Weeks two to four: what needs the personal identity code

If Migri grants you a residence permit, EU registration or a residence card, you are registered automatically and the code comes with the decision. Otherwise you request it from DVV with an online form and visit in person within one month, every family member included; it is free and takes two to three weeks in work and study cases. Tax offices in larger cities issue codes for tax purposes only, usually within one to three business days. Neither of those codes gives you a municipality of residence – for that you still apply to DVV, as part 3 explains.

...

| Mistake | What happens | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Assuming the code from Migri or Vero makes you a resident | No kotikunta, so no health station, school place or residence-based benefits | Apply for the municipality of residence at DVV |
| Submitting DVV’s form and forgetting the visit | The visit must take place within one month of the form, for every person | Book the appointment when you submit |
| EU citizen letting three months pass | You are staying without registering and cannot get a kotikunta | Apply to Migri within three months of arrival |

...

## What to do now

| Step | What | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Check your route to residence (part 2); legalise your certificates | Before you book the move |
| 2 | Secure an address | Before you register |
| 3 | Register your right of residence, or visit DVV as a Nordic citizen | Within three months, or one month for Nordic citizens |
| 4 | Request the personal identity code and the municipality of residence | Right after arrival; visit DVV within one month |
| 5 | Collect your tax card and open a bank account | Before your first payday |
| 6 | Notify Kela, register as a jobseeker if needed, find your health station | During your first weeks |
| 7 | Apply for the foreigner’s identity card online | Once the kotikunta is registered |

sources.title: EU Citizens: Registering Your Right of Residence in Finland | NordicExpat
highlights:
- You should apply before the three months are up, not after.

...

EU free movement does not give an unconditional right to settle indefinitely without any basis. To stay longer than three months, you need grounds for residence. According to Migri and InfoFinland, the qualifying grounds are:

- Work — you are employed or you are self-employed in Finland.
- Study — you are enrolled at an educational institution and can support yourself for the duration.
- Sufficient resources — you have enough means to support yourself (and family) without recourse to Finnish social assistance, plus health insurance coverage.
- Family ties — you are joining a family member who is an EU citizen exercising free movement in Finland.

The "sufficient resources" route matters for people who are not working straight away — early retirees, accompanying partners, or those job-hunting on savings. There is no single published income figure you must clear; Migri assesses sufficiency case by case, and you generally must not be reliant on social assistance. The health-insurance expectation is part of this test, which is worth bearing in mind during the gap before you are inside the Finnish system — travel or expat health cover can bridge that period until your residence and Kela coverage are sorted.

...

### 1. Apply online through Enter Finland

Create an account in the Enter Finland e-service (enterfinland.fi) and complete the application for registration of an EU citizen's right of residence. You attach digital copies of your supporting documents here. You pay the processing fee when you submit.

### 2. Pay the processing fee

According to Migri's fee schedule, the processing fee for registering an EU citizen's right of residence is 53 euros, and it is the same 53 euros whether you apply electronically or on paper (as of 2026 — confirm the current figure on migri.fi). For reference, Migri lists the same 53-euro fee for a residence card for a family member of an EU citizen and for a certificate of permanent right of residence.

### 3. Book an appointment and verify your identity in person

After submitting online, you book an appointment in Migri's appointment system (migri.vihta.com) and attend a Migri service point in person. The in-person visit is to prove your identity and present the originals of your attachments. Bring your valid passport or national identity card.

### 4. Show your grounds for residence

At the appointment, you present evidence of your basis for staying. Depending on your situation, that means:

- Employees: an employment contract or a written statement from your employer.
- Self-employed: documentation of your business, such as a trade register extract.
- Students: a certificate of study and an assurance of sufficient funds.
- Family members: a marriage certificate or other proof of the family relationship.

### 5. Receive your registration certificate

Once you have shown sufficient evidence, Migri issues a certificate of registration of your right of residence. As noted, it is valid until further notice. Keep it — you may be asked for it when dealing with other authorities.

...

Processing time depends heavily on your grounds and on whether your documentation is complete. Migri does not publish a single fixed processing time for EU registration the way it gives week-ranges for some other cases; for straightforward, well-documented applications a certificate can often be issued at or shortly after the in-person visit, while more complex cases take longer. Migri publishes current processing-time information per application type — check migri.fi for the up-to-date estimate for registrations before you plan anything time-sensitive around it. The practical takeaway: apply early, attach clean documents, and book the in-person appointment as soon as slots allow, because the appointment is often the real bottleneck rather than the decision itself.

...

## EU Registration vs. DVV vs. the Tax Office

A recurring source of confusion is that Finland makes you deal with three separate offices, and EU registration is only one of them. Keeping them distinct saves a lot of wasted trips:

- Migri confirms your right to reside (the EU registration in this guide).
- DVV runs the population register: it issues your personal identity code (henkilötunnus) and records your municipality of residence (kotikunta) if you are moving for at least a year. Registering with Migri does not automatically register you with DVV — these are different systems, and you must do the DVV step yourself.
- The Tax Administration (Verohallinto, via vero.fi/OmaVero) issues your tax card (verokortti), which everyone working in Finland needs.

Migri's FAQ is explicit that having a personal identity code does not, on its own, prove your right of residence — you still need the registration certificate. And conversely, the registration certificate is not a personal identity code. You will generally want all three: the registration, the henkilötunnus, and the tax card, in roughly that order of logical priority though they often overlap in practice.

In the Helsinki capital region, International House Helsinki brings several of these services under one roof, which can make the sequence less painful for newcomers in that area.

...

## Practical Tips Before You Apply

- Sort your documents before you start the online form. A clean employment contract, proof of study, or evidence of resources plus health insurance is what unblocks the whole process.
- Book the in-person appointment early. Slots in busy service points (Helsinki especially) can be the long pole; the online application and the 53-euro fee are quick by comparison.
- Do the DVV step too — don't assume Migri covers it. Your personal identity code and municipality of residence come from DVV, and without them, banking, healthcare and tax all stall.
- Mind the health-cover gap. Until your Finnish residence and Kela coverage are in place, you are expected to have health insurance, and it is also part of the "sufficient resources" grounds — interim travel or expat health cover is a sensible bridge.
- Keep the registration certificate safe. It is valid until further notice but you will be asked to produce it by other authorities, so store it where you can find it.

sources.title: Arrival at Aalto University | Aalto University
highlights:
### EU/EEA citizens: registering right of residence 

EU/EEA, Switzerland and Liechtenstein citizens do not need a residence permit, instead they register their right of residence at the Finnish Immigration Service. The registration is required if you are staying in Finland for over 90 days without leaving the country. You can also obtain the Finnish personal identity code in connection with the registration.

You can fill in the online application once your study right has started and then book the appointment to visit the service point in Helsinki. The Finnish Immigration Service point in Helsinki is very busy and when you book an appointment, the next available time may be several weeks or even a few months away. 

You can watch this video on how to fill in the application form in Enter Finland

...

I am an EU citizen and studying in Finland for six months. If I visit Estonia twice during the six months, do I need to register my right of residence in Finland? 

You do not need to do so if you do not stay in Finland without a break for over three months. If, for example, you arrive in Finland in January and travel outside Finland in March and May, you do not need to register your residence. Keep the receipt or tickets of your journey, in case you need to prove later that you travelled abroad.

...

By presenting the European Health Insurance Card, you can prove the right to medically necessary treatment in Finland. The card must be valid for the whole duration of your exchange. We strongly recommend purchasing private health insurance as well, because it is significantly easier and faster to make an appointment at a private clinic.

...

### Documents you may need 

When you come to Finland, please remember to bring with you at least:

- A valid passport (recommended over other forms of ID)
- The Letter of Admission from Aalto University
- Proof of your insurances

...

- Proof of financial means to support your stay (e.g. a certificate of an Erasmus grant)
- Prescriptions if you are on medication

It is also good to have with you a payment card and some cash (euros).

sources.title: Moving to and Living in Helsinki 2026 | ENB Consulting
highlights:
When relocating to Helsinki, the order of formalities matters: immigration status → DVV/personal identity code/municipality of residence → Vero → Kela → banking/strong authentication → housing/utilities → local services. International House Helsinki / Helsinki-info provides local guidance for international newcomers. A city guide does not replace permit or benefit rules; always verify personal eligibility with Migri, DVV, Vero and Kela.

...

Non-EU nationals should confirm the correct residence permit; EU citizens should check whether registration of the right of residence is required for stays over three months. Nordic rules are separate.

Common early bottlenecks include civil-status documents, legalisation/translation, DVV appointments, housing and bank KYC. Check marriage/birth-certificate requirements before arrival.

...

- Set up bank account and strong authentication

...

- Plan public transport / driving
- Apply early for daycare/school if needed
- Register with employment/integration services where relevant

...

International House Helsinki moved to Ratapihantie 7 in Pasila on 1 June 2026. The service ecosystem brings together guidance and services relating to Migri EU registration, DVV personal data/personal identity code/municipality registration, tax cards, employment and Kela matters.

These services generally do not make immigration decisions; they provide guidance on authorities, forms/appointments, housing, employment, education, daycare and everyday life.

...

### Checklist

- Confusing personal identity code with municipality of residence
- Assuming Kela starts automatically
- Delaying tax card
- Assuming bank KYC finishes immediately
- Leaving school/daycare too late
- Missing legalisation/translation of foreign civil-status documents
- Treating local guidance as a Migri/DVV decision-maker
- Choosing housing based only on rent
